Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short set of questions called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply a well-studied tool that helps us understand how mood and anxiety have been feeling for you over these first postpartum days and weeks.  

Everything you share stays confidential between you and your care team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you right now. We’ll go through ten gentle questions; each one asks about the past seven days. If any question ever feels hard to talk about, we can pause or re-word it together.  

Whenever you’re ready, we can start with the first question:  

Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[soft half-smile that fades quickly]

I can still laugh… just not as easily as before the baby came. When my husband tries to be funny, I’ll chuckle for a second, but it fades fast—like the joy doesn’t quite reach me. Mostly I’m too tired or preoccupied.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[gives a small nod]

Most of the time, yes—I can still laugh. It’s just… it feels a little forced sometimes. I’ll smile at something silly my husband says, but the laughter doesn’t feel as full or last as long as it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[slow exhale]

I do look forward to things—like bath-time with the baby, or my mom bringing dinner—but the excitement feels kind of muted. It’s more “I guess that’ll be nice” than the bubbly feeling I used to get.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[glancing down at my hands]

Sometimes. Like last night when she wouldn’t settle for two hours—I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong, maybe I ate too much chocolate or didn’t swaddle her tight enough. I know rationally babies just cry, but the thought still pops up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[fidgets with the edge of the baby blanket in my lap]

A few times, yeah. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart races, imagining she’s too quiet or her breathing looks odd—even though she’s fine. Nothing triggers it; it just shows up and sits in my chest until I check her ten times.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[quiet for a second]

Not full-on panic… more like this sudden wave of “what if something happens to her?” My chest gets tight and I have to peek into the bassinet to be sure she’s breathing. It passes after a minute, but it’s unsettling.
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a shaky breath]

Yes—some days it feels like the dirty bottles, laundry, and night feedings just pile up faster than I can handle them. I’ll start one chore, the baby cries, and suddenly I’m standing in the middle of the living room wanting to sit on the floor and cry myself.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It's more the other way around, I think. I lie down exhausted, but my mind keeps circling—did I sterilize the pump parts, is she breathing, will she wake up in 30 minutes anyway? I might drift off, then every squeak from the bassinet jerks me awake. So I'm sleeping maybe four broken hours a night, and no, it's not because I'm feeling desperately sad; it's just this restless, keyed-up buzz I can't switch off.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the time—not every minute, but it kind of rolls in like a fog. I’ll be folding her tiny clothes and suddenly feel weepy, thinking how fast she’s changing and how I’m too tired to enjoy it properly. It lifts for a while if someone visits or she gives me a smile, but yes, the low mood keeps coming back most days.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[shakes head slowly]

Not really. I’ve felt teary a couple of times—like when she wouldn’t latch at 3 a.m.—but the tears never quite fall. It’s more this pressure behind my eyes that never turns into actual crying.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[looking straight at you, voice steady]

No. That thought hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Brief Professional Note  

Identified symptoms / behavioral indicators  
- Dysthymic mood: intermittent sadness, “fog,” weepiness most days  
- Anhedonia: enjoyment markedly blunted; laughter feels forced  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame over infant care  
- Heightened, unprovoked anxiety with somatic arousal (heart racing, chest tightness)  
- Overwhelm / difficulty coping with routine tasks  
- Sleep disruption driven by intrusive worry, not solely infant demands  
- No current suicidal or self-harm ideation  

Pattern summary  
Persistent low/numbed affect and diminished pleasure, accompanied by prominent generalized and infant-focused anxiety, mild obsessional checking, sleep fragmentation, and self-criticism. Symptoms present “most days,” beginning post-delivery. No psychotic features or safety concerns elicited.

Screening significance  
Findings exceed “baby blues” threshold; meet provisional criteria for further evaluation of Major Depressive Episode with Peripartum Onset and comorbid anxiety. Recommend formal diagnostic interview (DSM-5-TR) and standardized tools (EPDS, GAD-7) to clarify severity and guide level-of-care decision.
